title: CSF Oligoclonal Bands: The Five Patterns and Intrathecal IgG
summary: Learn why oligoclonal bands are always read in paired CSF and serum, how isoelectric focusing with IgG immunoblotting defines a positive result, and how to tell the five consensus patterns apart, including the type 4 mirror and the type 5 monoclonal ladder.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 47 Hits 9–11, Exam Trap 1 and the OCB rows of the Number Vault, checked against Trbojevic-Cepe 2004 (describes the international consensus five patterns), Jin 2023, Hegen 2019, Schwenkenbecher 2018 and Rammohan 2009. The reviewer writes “IFE” for the CSF method, an acronym the chapter elsewhere uses for immunofixation; the sources describe isoelectric focusing (IEF) followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting or immunofixation, and the lesson uses that wording (register flag rv-ocb-ief-method). The reviewer links types 2 and 3 to multiple sclerosis; the sources stress these patterns are not MS-specific (register flag rv-ocb-not-ms-specific). The Freedman 2005 consensus paper cited by the reviewer is not open access and was not read; its recommendations are taught only where the open sources state them. Not taught: IgG index and synthesis-rate formulas, kappa free light chains, MALDI-TOF (Number Vault row 7), IVIG IFE pattern (Number Vault row 6; Hit 16).

objectives: Explain why oligoclonal bands must be tested in paired CSF and serum.
Classify CSF/serum results into the five consensus patterns and state which indicate intrathecal IgG synthesis.
Recognise the type 4 mirror pattern and the type 5 monoclonal ladder as findings that do not indicate intrathecal synthesis.

scenes.title: Bands in the CSF, but whose?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a 31-year-old with a first episode of optic neuritis has a lumbar puncture. The CSF and a serum sample drawn the same morning go for oligoclonal band testing. Two result strips are shown side by side: patient A has four CSF bands and none in serum; patient B has four CSF bands and the same four in serum. Question token: “Made in the brain, or copied from the blood?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a young adult with a first episode of optic neuritis has a lumbar puncture, and a serum sample is drawn the same morning.
Two possible results. Patient A: four bands in the cerebrospinal fluid, none in serum. Patient B: four bands in the fluid, and the same four in serum.
Both show bands in the spinal fluid. Do both mean the antibody was made inside the nervous system?

props.label: Made in the brain, or copied from the blood?

scenes.title: The five consensus patterns
scenes.altText: Five schematic cards, each showing a CSF lane and a serum lane. Type 1: no oligoclonal bands in either fluid (normal). Type 2: bands in CSF, absent from serum (CSF-restricted). Type 3: CSF-restricted bands PLUS additional bands identical in CSF and serum (a combination of types 2 and 4). Type 4: identical bands in CSF and serum (“mirror” pattern). Type 5: a monoclonal pattern identical in both fluids. Below: types 2 and 3 indicate intrathecal IgG synthesis; type 4 indicates a systemic immune response with bands reaching the CSF from blood; type 5 points to a plasma cell disorder.

cues.text: An international consensus describes five patterns, always reading spinal fluid and serum side by side. Type 1: no oligoclonal bands in either fluid.
Type 2: bands in the fluid that are absent from serum. Type 3: those fluid-only bands, plus extra bands that are identical in both. Both patterns indicate IgG made inside the central nervous system.
Type 4 is the mirror pattern: the same bands in both fluids. The response is systemic, and the bands reach the spinal fluid from the blood.
Type 5 is a monoclonal pattern in both fluids, which points to a plasma cell disorder such as a monoclonal gammopathy, not to synthesis in the nervous system.

scenes.title: Why the serum lane matters
scenes.altText: Schematic: a blood vessel and the CSF space separated by the blood-brain barrier. Left: B-cell clones inside the CNS secrete IgG that appears only in the CSF lane. Right: clones in the blood make IgG that crosses into the CSF, so the same bands appear in both lanes. Method card: isoelectric focusing (IEF) followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting or immunofixation is the reference method; CSF and serum are run in parallel with the same amount of IgG loaded; sensitive immunoblot methods detect bands in unconcentrated CSF. Positivity card: at least two CSF bands absent from serum (some laboratories require three; where three is the cut-off, one or two bands is a borderline pattern).

cues.text: Why does serum matter? Oligoclonal bands also form in blood, in many systemic disorders. Those bands can reach the spinal fluid across the blood-brain barrier, so a band in the fluid alone does not prove it was made there.
Only a band present in the spinal fluid and absent from serum shows local production. That is why the consensus calls parallel testing of fluid and serum imperative.

The reference method is isoelectric focusing, followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting or immunofixation, with the same amount of IgG loaded from each fluid. Sensitive blotting detects bands in unconcentrated spinal fluid.
A positive result needs at least two bands in the fluid that serum lacks. Some laboratories use three, which raises specificity; under that rule, one or two bands is a borderline pattern.

props.title: Clones inside the CNS
lines: IgG in the CSF lane only

scenes.title: Reading the strips
scenes.altText: Four practice strips (invented). Strip 1: three bands in CSF, none in serum → type 2, intrathecal synthesis. Strip 2: two CSF-only bands plus four bands shared with serum → type 3, intrathecal plus systemic. Strip 3: identical bands in both → type 4, systemic. Strip 4: an evenly spaced ladder of four or five bands of falling intensity, identical in both fluids → a monoclonal IgG on IEF, type 5; workup for a plasma cell disorder. Hook answers: patient A = type 2; patient B = type 4.

cues.text: Read four strips. Three bands in the fluid and none in serum: type 2. Two fluid-only bands plus four shared bands: type 3. Both show synthesis inside the nervous system.
Identical bands in both fluids: type 4, a systemic response that does not show intrathecal synthesis.

Watch the fourth strip. On isoelectric focusing a single monoclonal IgG can look like an evenly spaced ladder of four or five bands. When that ladder is identical in both fluids, it is type 5, not many clones.
Back to the hook. Patient A is type 2, made in the nervous system. Patient B is type 4, copied from the blood.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Identical bands in CSF and serum confirm intrathecal synthesis” (✓ that is type 4, a systemic response); “CSF-restricted bands prove multiple sclerosis” (✓ types 2 and 3 also occur in CNS infections, autoimmune encephalitis and other inflammatory disorders; interpret with the clinical picture); “A ladder of bands is oligoclonal” (✓ on IEF one monoclonal IgG can form a ladder of four to five evenly spaced bands; identical in both fluids = type 5).

cues.text: Trap one: identical bands in fluid and serum confirm intrathecal synthesis. No: that is type 4, a systemic response.
Trap two: fluid-only bands prove multiple sclerosis. No: infections of the nervous system and other inflammatory or autoimmune disorders produce them too.
Trap three: a ladder of bands is oligoclonal. No: one monoclonal IgG can focus as an evenly spaced ladder. Identical in both fluids, it is type 5.

props.title: ✗ “A ladder of bands is oligoclonal.”
lines: ✓ One monoclonal IgG; both fluids = type 5

scenes.title: Original, photocopy, rubber stamp
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Bands the serum lacks are ORIGINALS written in the CNS (types 2 and 3). Bands identical in both fluids are a PHOTOCOPY from the blood (type 4). One clone’s ladder in both fluids is a RUBBER STAMP (type 5).” Tokens: original = 2, 3 · photocopy = 4 · stamp = 5. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: bands the serum lacks are originals, written inside the nervous system: types 2 and 3. Identical bands in both fluids are a photocopy from the blood: type 4. One clone in both fluids is a rubber stamp: type 5.

Where it breaks: an original does not name the disease, since infections and autoimmune disorders write them too; cut-offs differ between laboratories, and one or two bands can be borderline; and a single focused band can still contain more than one clone.

props.title: Where it breaks

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Paired CSF + serum, IEF + IgG immunoblot · ≥2 CSF-restricted bands = positive”, “Types 2, 3 = intrathecal · 4 = systemic mirror · 5 = monoclonal”.

cues.text: Always read oligoclonal bands in paired spinal fluid and serum, because only bands the serum lacks, types 2 and 3, show IgG made in the nervous system, while identical bands, type 4, and a monoclonal pattern in both fluids, type 5, do not.

props.label: Paired CSF + serum · IEF + IgG blot · ≥ 2 CSF-only bands

explanation.what: Plain language: in a nervous-system inflammation, a few B-cell families can settle inside the brain and spinal cord and make their own antibodies. On a gel these show as a few sharp bands. Because antibodies from the blood also leak into spinal fluid, the lab runs a serum sample next to the fluid: only bands the blood does not have were made inside. Scientific terms: oligoclonal bands (OCB), intrathecal IgG synthesis, blood-brain barrier, isoelectric focusing (IEF), IgG-specific immunoblotting/immunofixation, CSF-restricted bands, mirror pattern, monoclonal pattern.
explanation.why: Many systemic disorders make oligoclonal IgG in serum, and it can enter the CSF across the blood-brain barrier, so a band in CSF alone cannot locate its source. Comparing with paired serum, loaded at the same IgG amount, separates local synthesis (bands absent from serum) from passive transfer (identical bands).
explanation.measure: Reference method: IEF followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting or immunofixation, CSF and serum in parallel with equal IgG; sensitive blotting works on unconcentrated CSF. Positive: at least two CSF bands absent from serum (some laboratories use three; in Hegen 2019’s pooled studies, specificity was about 92% with a cut-off of two and 97% with three). Where three is the cut-off, one or two CSF-restricted bands is a borderline pattern (Hegen 2019). Five patterns: 1 none; 2 CSF-restricted; 3 CSF-restricted plus identical bands; 4 identical (mirror); 5 monoclonal in both.
explanation.differs: Types 2 and 3 (intrathecal synthesis) vs type 4 (systemic response, bands from blood) vs type 5 (monoclonal IgG, plasma cell disorder). On IEF a monoclonal IgG can appear as an evenly spaced ladder of four to five bands, which is not oligoclonal. CSF-restricted bands support multiple sclerosis but also occur in CNS infections, autoimmune encephalitis and other inflammatory disorders.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the pattern from a CSF/serum description, pick which patterns indicate intrathecal synthesis, explain why paired serum is required, or reject “identical bands = intrathecal synthesis”.

mnemonic.text: Bands the serum lacks are ORIGINALS written in the CNS (types 2 and 3); identical bands in both fluids are a PHOTOCOPY from the blood (type 4); one clone’s ladder in both fluids is a RUBBER STAMP (type 5).
mnemonic.explanation: Ties each pattern to where the IgG was made.
mnemonic.limitation: An “original” does not name the disease (infections and autoimmune disorders produce CSF-restricted bands too); cut-offs vary by laboratory, and where three is the cut-off one or two bands is borderline; a single focused band can contain products of more than one clone.

analogyLimitations: Band strips are schematic, not real gels.
The five-pattern scheme is a consensus reporting convention; laboratory cut-offs and methods differ.
takeaway: Always read oligoclonal bands in paired spinal fluid and serum, because only bands the serum lacks, types 2 and 3, show IgG made in the nervous system, while identical bands, type 4, and a monoclonal pattern in both fluids, type 5, do not.

questions.stem: Isoelectric focusing with IgG immunoblotting shows four bands in a patient’s CSF and no bands in the paired serum. Which pattern is this, and what does it indicate?

options.rationale: Correct. Bands present in CSF and absent from serum show IgG made within the CNS.

options.text: Type 4: systemic response with transfer into CSF
options.rationale: Incorrect. Type 4 requires identical bands in serum, and the serum here has none.
Incorrect. Type 5 is a monoclonal pattern present in both fluids.
Incorrect. Type 1 has no oligoclonal bands in either fluid.

questions.stem: A CSF sample and its paired serum show the same five oligoclonal bands, with no extra bands in the CSF. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Type 4: a systemic immune response; intrathecal synthesis is not shown
options.rationale: Correct. Identical bands in both fluids reflect oligoclonal IgG from the blood reaching the CSF.
Incorrect. Type 3 needs additional CSF bands that serum lacks.

options.text: Positive for intrathecal synthesis because five bands exceed the cut-off of two
options.rationale: Incorrect. The cut-off counts CSF bands ABSENT from serum; here there are none.
Incorrect. Type 5 is a single monoclonal IgG, which on IEF can appear as an evenly spaced ladder, not several unrelated oligoclonal bands.

questions.stem: Why must a serum sample be tested in parallel with CSF for oligoclonal bands?

options.text: Serum oligoclonal IgG can enter the CSF across the blood-brain barrier, so only CSF bands absent from serum show local synthesis
options.rationale: Correct. Parallel testing separates intrathecal synthesis from passive transfer.

options.text: Serum is needed to concentrate the CSF before focusing
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serum does not concentrate CSF; sensitive immunoblot methods detect bands in unconcentrated CSF.

options.text: Serum bands confirm the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bands shared with serum indicate a systemic response, not MS.

options.text: Serum is the positive control for the IgG antibody stain
options.rationale: Incorrect. The serum lane is the patient’s own comparison sample, used to locate the source of each band.

references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Trbojevic-Cepe M. Detection of Oligoclonal Ig Bands: Clinical Significance and Trends in Methodological Improvement. EJIFCC. 2004;15(3):86-94.
references.usedFor: International consensus: IEF with IgG-specific immunofixation as the most sensitive/standard method with equal IgG in parallel CSF and serum; parallel analysis imperative because serum oligoclonal IgG can enter CSF across the barrier; definition of at least two CSF bands absent from serum; the five patterns (type 3 = combination of 2 and 4; type 5 = monoclonal in myeloma/MGUS); monoclonal IgG as a 4–5-band ladder on IEF; a single IEF band may contain several clones; type 4 as systemic immune activation; OCB in non-MS disorders.

references.citation: Jin H, Lu Q, Gao F, Hao H. Application of oligoclonal bands and other cerebrospinal fluid variables in multiple sclerosis and other neuroimmunological diseases: a narrative review. Ann Transl Med. 2023;11(7):282. doi:10.21037/atm-21-3073
references.usedFor: Five patterns with interpretations (types 2 and 3 indicate intrathecal synthesis; type 4 mirror pattern; type 5 monoclonal, plasma cell disease, not intrathecal synthesis); IEF with IgG-specific staining as gold standard; CSF-restricted bands also seen in autoimmune encephalitis, connective tissue disease and infections (tuberculosis, syphilis, HIV, viral encephalitis); notes that Jin abbreviates isoelectric focusing electrophoresis as IFE.

references.citation: Hegen H, Zinganell A, Auer M, Deisenhammer F. The clinical significance of single or double bands in cerebrospinal fluid isoelectric focusing. A retrospective study and systematic review. PLoS One. 2019;14(4):e0215410. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0215410
references.usedFor: IEF with immunoblotting as gold standard; cut-offs of ≥2 vs ≥3 CSF-restricted bands with pooled specificity about 92% vs 97%; 1–2 CSF-restricted bands as a borderline pattern (defined against a ≥3 cut-off) of moderate significance.

references.citation: Schwenkenbecher P, Konen FF, Wurster U, et al. The Persisting Significance of Oligoclonal Bands in the Dawning Era of Kappa Free Light Chains for the Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis. Int J Mol Sci. 2018;19(12):E3796. doi:10.3390/ijms19123796
references.usedFor: OCB determination as the gold standard for intrathecal IgG synthesis; requires methodological expertise and may be rater-dependent; positive criterion of two bands in CSF only.

references.citation: Rammohan KW. Cerebrospinal fluid in multiple sclerosis. Ann Indian Acad Neurol. 2009;12(4):246-253. doi:10.4103/0972-2327.58282
references.usedFor: Immunoblot after isoelectric focusing on unconcentrated CSF with paired, diluted serum so CSF and serum IgG profiles can be compared; mirror pattern (identical bands) indicating a systemic immune response.

claims.text: Five consensus patterns of paired CSF/serum oligoclonal IgG and their meaning.
Paired serum is required because serum oligoclonal IgG can enter CSF; only CSF bands absent from serum show intrathecal synthesis.
IEF followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting/immunofixation is the reference method, with equal IgG in parallel CSF and serum; sensitive blotting detects bands in unconcentrated CSF.
Positivity: at least two CSF-restricted bands; some laboratories use three (specificity about 92% vs 97% in pooled studies); one or two bands borderline where three is the cut-off.
A monoclonal IgG on IEF can appear as a ladder of four to five evenly spaced bands; a single IEF band may contain several clones.
CSF-restricted bands also occur in CNS infections, autoimmune encephalitis and other inflammatory disorders.
Reviewer attributes the MS workup recommendations to the Freedman et al. 2005 consensus.
claims.note: Freedman 2005 (Arch Neurol) is not open access and was not read; the attribution is not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 47 Hit 11 says the MS workup uses “IFE” on unconcentrated CSF without naming isoelectric focusing. Elsewhere in Ch. 47 (Hits 8, 12, 13, 16) “IFE” means immunofixation electrophoresis, while Jin 2023 uses “IFE” for isoelectric focusing electrophoresis, so the acronym is ambiguous. The open sources describe the reference method as isoelectric focusing followed by IgG-specific immunoblotting or immunofixation, with CSF and serum loaded at equal IgG; Trbojevic-Cepe 2004 says high-resolution zone electrophoresis with immunofixation is inferior to IEF with immunofixation (register flag rv-ocb-ief-method).

Ch. 47 Hit 9 presents types 2 and 3 as supporting multiple sclerosis. Jin 2023 and Trbojevic-Cepe 2004 stress that CSF-restricted bands also occur in CNS infections, autoimmune encephalitis, connective tissue disease and other inflammatory disorders, so they indicate intrathecal synthesis, not MS specifically (register flag rv-ocb-not-ms-specific).

morphology.note: No gel images; band patterns shown as schematic cards.
